stem: Your CI review posts comment-accuracy findings on every pull request and developers dismiss 41% of them. Two sprints ago you added "be conservative and only report high-confidence findings" to the review prompt; the dismissal rate moved from 44% to 41%. What change is most likely to actually raise precision?

options.text: Instruct the model to assign each finding a confidence score from 1 to 10 and post only findings scoring 8 or above.
Keep the prompt as it is and have a rotating reviewer triage the findings before they are posted to the pull request.
Move the review to a larger model, on the view that comment accuracy is a judgment the current model handles poorly.
Replace the confidence wording with a rule: flag a comment only when it contradicts the code it documents.

explanation: Vague confidence qualifiers give the model no decision boundary. A categorical criterion states exactly what condition makes a finding reportable, which is what moves precision.

why.A: Self-reported confidence is the same vague qualifier with a number attached, and the model is already confident in the findings developers dismiss.
why.B: Shifts the triage burden onto a human every day and leaves the noisy prompt generating the same findings.
why.C: A larger model still has to guess which comment discrepancies are worth reporting, because the prompt never states the boundary.

stem: Your CI review runs four finding categories. Over the last month: security 89% accepted, correctness 81% accepted, performance 76% accepted, naming and style 12% accepted. Naming and style accounts for 63% of all posted comments. Developers have started collapsing the whole review thread without reading it, and two genuine security findings reached main unread last week. What should you do first?

options.text: Cap the review at the five highest-severity findings per pull request so the thread stays short enough to read.
Ask developers to record a dismissal reason on every naming and style comment so you can improve that prompt from real data.
Disable the naming and style category while you rewrite its criteria, leaving the three trusted categories running.
Keep all four categories but post naming and style findings at a lower severity so developers can skip them.

explanation: One high false positive category is burying the categories that work and eroding trust in all of them. Removing it immediately restores signal while its criteria are fixed offline.

why.A: A volume cap leaves the 88% false positive rate in naming and style untouched, and the model's own severity ranking then decides which real findings get dropped.
why.B: Useful telemetry, but it leaves the noisy category running for weeks while trust keeps eroding.
why.D: The comments are still posted, so they still bury the accurate findings in the same thread.

stem: The same class of finding, a missing null check on a request parameter, was reported as "critical" on one pull request and "minor" on another in the same week. The prompt says: "Assign each finding a severity of critical, major or minor based on its impact." What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Define each severity level with explicit criteria and a concrete code example of a finding at that level.
Post findings without a severity and let the reviewing developer assign one at triage.
Reduce the scale to two levels, blocking and non-blocking, so there is less room for disagreement.
Have the model output a numeric impact score from 1 to 100 and derive severity from thresholds.

explanation: "Based on its impact" is not a decision boundary. Explicit criteria plus a worked code example per level give the model something concrete to classify against, which is what produces consistent severity.

why.B: Shifts the classification work onto developers instead of fixing the prompt.
why.C: Fewer buckets with the same undefined boundary still splits identical findings across runs.
why.D: Renames the problem: the model now has to invent an equally undefined number.

stem: Your CI review posts about 22 findings on the average pull request and developers act on 6. You are rewriting the review prompt to cut false positives. Which two edits directly address precision? (Select 2)

options.text: State which categories to report, bugs and security, and which to skip, minor style and local conventions.
Add "report only findings you are highly confident about" to the output instructions so borderline ones drop out.
Replace "check the error handling" with "flag a catch block only when it swallows the exception without logging or rethrowing".
Add "be conservative, this is a busy team and review noise is expensive" above the review criteria block.

explanation: Both edits give the model a categorical boundary: which classes of issue to report, and the exact condition that makes a finding reportable. Precision comes from criteria, not adjectives.

why.B: Confidence filtering is the instruction that repeatedly fails to move precision, because model confidence is not calibrated to developer agreement.
why.D: A tone instruction with no decision boundary attached to it.

stem: Your CI test-generation step suggests roughly 30 tests per pull request and developers keep about 4 of them. Four candidate lines are proposed for the prompt. Which one is most likely to reduce the low-value suggestions?

options.text: Suggest a test only for a branch, error path or boundary no test in the provided files exercises.
Suggest only tests that you judge to be genuinely valuable, and skip anything of low value.
Have the model score each suggestion for value and post them ranked, so developers read the best ones first.
Limit the output to at most eight test suggestions per pull request so reviewers are not flooded with them.

explanation: A names the exact condition that makes a suggestion worth posting and anchors it to evidence already in context, the existing test files. The others are qualifiers, orderings or caps with no criterion behind them.

why.B: "Genuinely valuable" is the judgment the prompt is supposed to define, not delegate.
why.C: Ranking changes the order in which low-value suggestions appear; it does not change how many the model produces.
why.D: A cap changes the volume, not the proportion of low-value suggestions, and it can drop the good ones.

stem: Your support agent flags conversations for QA using the instruction "flag any conversation that seems unusual". It now flags 300 of the 1,100 daily conversations and the QA team has stopped opening the queue. What is the correct change?

options.text: Have the agent score each conversation for risk from 1 to 100 and flag only the highest-scoring 5% each day.
Replace it with named triggers: an above-threshold refund, an unsourced policy answer, or a request restated three times.
Keep the instruction and have QA review a random sample of 30 flagged conversations a day to clear the queue.
Add "only flag conversations you are confident are genuinely problematic" and re-measure the volume next week.

explanation: Named, checkable trigger conditions replace an undefined word, so flag volume tracks real risk rather than the model's sense of what is unusual.

why.A: A self-reported risk number is no better calibrated than "unusual", and a fixed 5% cap has no relation to how many conversations actually need review.
why.C: Reduces reviewer load without improving which conversations reach the queue.
why.D: Another undefined qualifier, and the agent already believes each flag is warranted.

stem: Your CI review returns findings through a JSON schema, so every finding has file, line, issue, severity and suggested_fix. The keys are always present but the content varies wildly: suggested_fix is sometimes a concrete replacement expression and sometimes "consider refactoring this", and issue is sometimes one clause and sometimes three paragraphs. The prompt already contains a paragraph describing the desired style. What is the most effective next step?

options.text: Post-process every finding through a second model call that rewrites it into the house style before posting.
Tighten the JSON schema with a maxLength on issue and a pattern constraint on suggested_fix so fields stay terse.
Expand the prose in the prompt describing what a good suggested_fix looks like.
Add two or three few-shot examples of complete findings showing the detail wanted in each field.

explanation: Few-shot examples are the reliable way to communicate a format that prose instructions have already failed to convey. The model matches the demonstrated shape instead of interpreting an adjective.

why.A: Adds a call and a failure point to fix something the first call does correctly once it is shown an example.
why.B: The schema constrains shape and length, not whether the text is specific and actionable.
why.C: More of the instruction that has already produced inconsistent results.

stem: Your test-coverage reviewer is inconsistent on one class of case: when a function has an if/else and only the if branch is tested, it sometimes reports a coverage gap and sometimes calls the function covered. Both behaviours appear on near-identical code in the same week. The team does not want every untested branch reported either, since defensive branches that cannot be reached in production are deliberately left alone. What addresses this most directly?

options.text: Add a rule stating that a function counts as covered only when every branch in it has a test exercising it.
Add two to four few-shot examples of this exact case, each showing why it was or was not counted as a gap.
Run the coverage tool first and pass its line-coverage report to the model instead of the source files.
Switch the reviewer to a model with a larger context window so it can hold the whole function and all of its callers in view while judging.

explanation: The failure is an ambiguous judgment boundary, which is what a small number of worked examples is for. Showing the reasoning lets the model apply the same judgment to branch shapes you never enumerated.

why.A: A blanket rule buys consistency by flagging the defensive and unreachable branches the team has said it does not want reported.
why.C: Line coverage from a tool answers a different question than whether an untested branch matters.
why.D: The inconsistency shows up on near-identical code the model already holds in full, so context capacity is not the failing part.

stem: To stop the reviewer flagging accepted patterns, your team added 25 few-shot examples, each naming one specific construct that must not be flagged: this retry wrapper, this context manager, this error swallow in the metrics module. Those 25 constructs are never flagged now, but a new retry wrapper written on the same principle in a different module is still reported as a bug. What is wrong with the current examples?

options.text: The examples belong in CLAUDE.md, where they load on every run, rather than inside the review prompt.
They enumerate exceptions instead of showing the reasoning that separates an accepted pattern from a genuine issue.
The examples are not ordered by how often each construct appears, so the common ones get least attention.
Twenty-five examples exceed what the model can attend to, so the later ones are effectively ignored.

explanation: Few-shot works by demonstrating judgment. Enumerated exceptions teach only the enumerated cases, while two to four examples that show why a pattern was accepted generalise to novel patterns of the same kind.

why.A: Moving the same enumeration to a file that loads every run does not make any of it generalise to a new construct.
why.C: Ordering does not change the fact that no example explains the underlying reasoning.
why.D: The listed constructs are all handled correctly, so attention is not the failing part.

stem: Your document analysis subagent extracts claim and source pairs from research papers. It performs well on papers with a numbered bibliography and superscript markers, but on papers using inline parenthetical citations such as (Okonjo et al., 2024, p. 17), it returns an empty source on 34% of claims. A sizeable part of the corpus uses both styles in the same paper. The prompt already describes both citation styles in prose. What is the most effective fix?

options.text: Make the source field required in the schema so an empty value can no longer be returned for any claim.
Detect the citation style with a regular expression and route each paper to a prompt written for that style.
Add a few-shot example of correct extraction for each structure: inline parenthetical and numbered bibliography.
Instruct the subagent to search the entire document for a bibliography section before giving up and returning an empty source value.

explanation: Varied document structure is the case few-shot examples handle best. A correct extraction shown for each structure teaches the model what a citation looks like in each, which the prose description has not achieved.

why.A: A required field with no recognised value present pressures the model to fabricate a source, which is worse than an empty one.
why.B: Builds a routing layer for something one prompt with examples handles, and many papers mix both styles.
why.D: The sources are inline, so looking harder for a bibliography that does not exist changes nothing.

stem: Your invoice extraction returns null for payment_terms on 18% of documents. In those documents the terms are present but phrased in ways earlier samples did not contain: "Net 30 from date of issue", "due on receipt", "2/10 net 45". The field is nullable and the model is correctly instructed to return null when the value is absent. What is the right fix?

options.text: Make payment_terms required so the model has to produce a value.
Add few-shot examples showing payment terms extracted from each of these phrasings.
Attach the validation message "payment_terms was null" and retry each of these documents.
Add a regular expression to the schema matching common payment-term phrasings.

explanation: The information is present but expressed in formats the model has not been shown. Examples of correct extraction from varied phrasings fix recognition while preserving nullable behaviour for documents that genuinely have no terms.

why.A: Removes the model's honest way of reporting absence and invites fabrication on invoices that truly state no terms.
why.C: The retry message adds no information about how these phrasings map to the field, so it re-rolls the same judgment.
why.D: A schema pattern rejects values, it does not help the model recognise them in the source.

stem: Your team is triaging fixes for the extraction pipeline. Which two problems are appropriately solved by adding few-shot examples? (Select 2)

options.text: About 3% of responses fail to parse because the model wraps its JSON in a markdown fence, and output-format examples have not driven that to zero.
The model returns null for a quantity that is present but written informally, such as "a couple of pallets".
The model occasionally answers with a prose summary instead of calling the extraction tool at all.
The model is inconsistent about whether a delivery note appended to a purchase order is a separate document.

explanation: Few-shot examples address recognition of varied source formats and genuinely ambiguous judgment calls, both cases the instructions cannot fully specify in advance.

why.A: A syntax problem, eliminated by returning the data through tool_use with a JSON schema rather than parsing text.
why.C: Solved deterministically by tool_choice "any" or a forced tool, not by examples.

stem: Your support agent's tool descriptions were rewritten last month with input formats, example queries and boundaries, and misrouting fell from 14% to 3%. The remaining failures are genuinely ambiguous openers such as "I need to sort out the thing from last month" and "my account is wrong", where the agent picks get_customer or lookup_order roughly at random. What is the proportionate next step?

options.text: Add a routing classifier that reads the opening message and pre-selects the agent's tool.
Merge get_customer and lookup_order into one lookup tool that accepts any identifier.
Expand the tool descriptions further with more example queries covering vague and indirect openers.
Add two to four few-shot examples of ambiguous openers showing which tool was called first and why.

explanation: The descriptions have already been fixed and the residual failures are genuine ambiguity, which is exactly what a few targeted examples showing reasoning are for.

why.A: Over-engineered infrastructure for a residual 3%, and it bypasses the model's language understanding.
why.B: A large architectural change that still does not decide which backend an ambiguous request needs.
why.C: The descriptions are already comprehensive, and missing description detail is not what these failures are caused by.

stem: Your extraction service asks for JSON in the prompt and parses the response text. About 6% of responses fail to parse: a leading "Here is the extracted data:", a markdown fence, or a trailing comment after the closing brace. Your current mitigation is a chain of string repairs before json.loads. What is the correct fix?

options.text: Define an extraction tool whose input schema is the target structure and read the data from the tool_use block.
Ask for a flatter output structure with fewer nested objects so there is less JSON for the model to get wrong.
Add "Return only raw JSON, with no preamble, no code fence and no trailing commentary" to the system prompt, and re-measure the parse rate.
Keep the text response and add a repair step that sends malformed JSON back for the model to fix.

explanation: Tool use with a JSON schema is the reliable mechanism for schema-compliant output. The data arrives as structured tool input rather than as text you have to parse, which removes this class of failure entirely.

why.B: Flattening the structure does not stop a preamble or a code fence appearing around it.
why.C: A prompt instruction lowers the rate but leaves a non-zero failure rate on every request.
why.D: Spends an extra call per failure to patch a problem that does not have to occur at all.

stem: After moving to tool_use with a strict JSON schema, parse failures went to zero. A month of downstream reconciliation then shows that on 4% of invoices the line items do not add up to the extracted total, and on 1% the vendor's address sits in the customer_address field. A colleague concludes the schema is not being enforced. How should you respond?

options.text: Mark more fields as required so the model has less freedom to leave a value in the wrong place.
Switch tool_choice from "auto" to "any", on the view that "auto" applies the schema less strictly.
The schema guarantees shape and types, not correct values; add cross-field semantic checks.
Add regular expression patterns to the address fields so misplaced values are rejected during validation.

explanation: A strict schema eliminates syntax and type errors. Wrong values in correctly typed fields are semantic errors, and catching them takes explicit validation across fields or against the source.

why.A: Required fields control presence, not correctness, and they push the model to invent values when the source has none.
why.B: tool_choice governs whether and which tool is called, not how strictly the schema is applied.
why.D: Both entries are valid addresses, so a pattern cannot tell which one belongs in which field.

stem: Your pipeline receives a mixed stream of invoices, receipts and purchase orders with no reliable type marker, so you define three extraction tools, one per document type, and let the model pick. On roughly 9% of documents it answers with a prose description of the document instead of calling any tool, and the pipeline records an empty extraction. What is the correct configuration?

options.text: Leave tool_choice as "auto" and add "You must always call one of the provided tools" to the system prompt.
Collapse the three tools into one tool carrying every field from all three types, most of them optional.
Set tool_choice to a forced selection of extract_invoice, since invoices are the most common document type in the incoming stream.
Set tool_choice to "any", which requires a tool call while leaving the choice of tool to the model.

explanation: "any" is exactly this case: structured output is mandatory, but which schema applies depends on the document, and only the model can determine that after reading it.

why.A: "auto" permits a text answer by design, and a prompt instruction leaves a non-zero failure rate.
why.B: It leaves tool_choice at "auto", so prose answers keep happening, and it discards the type-specific validation the three schemas give you.
why.C: Forces the invoice schema onto receipts and purchase orders.

stem: Every document must have extract_metadata run against it first, because the enrichment tools need the issuer and effective date to look up the right reference data. In about 15% of runs the model calls an enrichment tool first and the lookup fails. You need the metadata extraction to be the first call of the request. What is the correct mechanism?

options.text: State in the system prompt that extract_metadata must always be called before any enrichment tool.
Set tool_choice to "any" so the first turn is guaranteed to be a tool call rather than a text answer.
Set tool_choice to {"type": "tool", "name": "extract_metadata"} on the first request, then enrich in later turns.
List extract_metadata first in the tools array, since the model works through the array in order.

explanation: Forced tool selection names the tool the model must call, which is the deterministic way to guarantee a particular extraction runs first. The remaining steps then proceed in later turns.

why.A: A prompt instruction is probabilistic, and it is what is already failing 15% of the time.
why.B: "any" guarantees that some tool is called, not which one.
why.D: The order of the tools array carries no execution semantics.

stem: purchase_order_number is a required string in your invoice schema. Roughly 30% of the invoices you process come from vendors who do not use purchase orders, and on those the model returns plausible values such as "PO-2025-0417" that appear nowhere in the document. What is the correct schema change?

options.text: Add "Never invent a purchase order number" to the extraction prompt and leave the field required.
Have the model write an empty string into the required field whenever no number is visible.
Make purchase_order_number optional and nullable, and say in the prompt that null means the document has none.
Add a validation step that rejects any value not matching the vendor's known purchase order format.

explanation: A required field tells the model that a value must exist. When the source frequently has none, the schema itself creates the pressure to fabricate, and a nullable field removes it.

why.A: The instruction contradicts the schema, and the schema constraint is the stronger signal.
why.B: An empty string still satisfies the required field, so the schema keeps saying a value must exist, and downstream cannot tell a vendor that issues no purchase orders from an extraction that found nothing.
why.D: Vendors without purchase orders have no known format, and a well-formed invented number passes the check anyway.

stem: Each finding your document analysis subagent returns carries a source_type enum: journal_article, preprint, conference_paper, government_report, news_article. Reviewing last month's output, a standards body specification was classified as government_report, a company engineering blog post as news_article, and a dataset landing page as journal_article. Downstream, the report generator weights credibility by source_type. What is the right schema change?

options.text: Extend the enum with standards_specification, technical_blog and dataset, and extend it again each time an unexpected new type appears.
Add an "other" value with a required detail string, plus "unclear" for sources that cannot be classified.
Keep the enum and instruct the subagent to pick the closest match and note any doubt in the finding text.
Replace the enum with a free-text source_type string so any description of the source can be recorded.

explanation: "other" with a detail string keeps the vocabulary stable for downstream weighting while giving the model a truthful place for anything the list does not cover, and "unclear" stops forced guesses on ambiguous sources.

why.A: An enumeration extended on discovery always lags the next unexpected source type, and every change ripples downstream.
why.C: This is the current behaviour: forcing the closest match is what produced the misclassifications, and prose notes are not read by the weighting step.
why.D: Free text destroys the stable vocabulary the report generator weights on and creates a normalisation problem in its place.

stem: Your schema requires contract_start_date as an ISO 8601 date. Validation rejects about 12% of extractions because the model returns the source's own formatting: "3/4/25", "4 March 2025" and "March 4th, 2025" all appear in the corpus, and some documents come from regions that write the day first. What is the best design?

options.text: Keep the strict schema and add prompt rules for normalising to ISO 8601, including region-specific numeric dates.
Leave the prompt and schema unchanged and retry each failed extraction until an ISO 8601 date comes back.
Change contract_start_date to a free-text string and normalise the dates in the downstream service instead.
Add a pattern to the schema that accepts all three observed formats so validation stops rejecting them.

explanation: The schema states the target format and the prompt supplies the conversion rules while the document and its region are still in context. That pairing is what handles inconsistent source formatting.

why.B: A retry with no new instructions re-rolls the same ambiguity and will never resolve day and month ordering reliably.
why.C: The downstream service has neither the document nor the region, so it cannot resolve "3/4/25".
why.D: This makes validation accept inconsistent values instead of producing one canonical format.

stem: Your CI job calls the API directly with two tools: report_findings, whose input schema defines the findings array your bot posts, and fetch_file_context. Which two statements about this setup are correct? (Select 2)

options.text: Setting tool_choice to "any" guarantees that report_findings is the specific tool that gets called on every run of the job.
The schema guarantees that each finding's line number corresponds to the code described in its issue text.
Returning findings through the tool's input schema removes JSON syntax errors from the failure modes to handle.
With tool_choice set to "auto", the model may answer with text instead of calling report_findings.

explanation: A schema delivered through tool use guarantees well-formed, correctly typed output, and "auto" leaves the model free to answer in text. Both are properties the pipeline has to be designed around.

why.A: "any" guarantees that some tool is called. Naming a specific tool requires forced tool selection.
why.B: Field types are guaranteed; whether the values in them are right is a semantic question no schema can answer.

stem: When Pydantic validation fails, your pipeline resends the identical request. That blind retry succeeds on 21% of attempts. Inspecting the failures, most are structural: an amount returned as "$1,240.00" where the schema wants a number, or a shipping address placed in billing_address. How should the retry be changed?

options.text: Send a follow-up with the original document, the failed extraction and the specific validation error.
Increase the retry count from one to five so more attempts get a chance to land a valid extraction.
Loosen the schema so these values validate, and normalise the formats in a later pipeline step.
Add "Be careful to follow the schema exactly" to the system prompt and keep the single blind retry.

explanation: A blind retry gives the model nothing it did not have the first time. Attaching the exact validation error alongside the document and its own failed output turns the retry into a correction task, which is where format and placement errors get fixed.

why.B: Five blind attempts is the same coin flip five times at five times the cost.
why.C: Loosening validation hides the errors instead of correcting them, and a swapped address cannot be recovered by a later step that no longer has the document.
why.D: A general instruction does not tell the model which field failed on this particular document.

stem: Your document analysis subagent must return publication_date for every finding. On preprint server pages the date is present and extraction works. On a batch of PDFs supplied by a partner the date appears nowhere in the file; it exists only in the partner's catalogue, which the subagent has never been given. The pipeline retries these three times with the validation error attached, then fails them. What is the right change?

options.text: Add few-shot examples showing publication dates extracted from PDFs with unusual layouts and cover pages.
Let the subagent estimate the date from the paper's content and flag the value as approximate for reviewers.
Raise the retry limit and add "the date must be somewhere in the document, please look again more carefully" to the retry prompt each time.
Stop retrying this class: return publication_date null with a note that the source omits it, or supply the catalogue.

explanation: Retry with error feedback fixes format and structural mistakes. It cannot produce information that is not in the input, so the correct response is to stop paying for retries and either accept a null or supply the missing source.

why.A: Examples teach recognition of formats that are present, and nothing in these PDFs contains the date in any format.
why.B: An estimated date presented as data corrupts downstream temporal reasoning; it is fabrication with a label attached.
why.C: More attempts at an absent value yield the same failure or a fabricated date.

stem: Reconciliation finds that on 4% of invoices the extracted line items do not sum to the extracted total. Some are extraction errors and some are genuine arithmetic mistakes by the vendor, and today both flow silently into the ledger. What extraction design surfaces the difference?

options.text: Reject any extraction where the two totals disagree and retry the document up to three times before failing it.
Instruct the model to check the arithmetic itself and return a single corrected total figure per invoice.
Return calculated_total from the line items beside stated_total from the document, with a conflict_detected flag.
Drop the total field from the schema and compute the invoice total downstream from the line items.

explanation: Returning both numbers with an explicit conflict flag preserves what the document says and what its own line items imply, which is the only way a later step can tell an extraction error from a vendor error.

why.A: The discrepancy is often in the source itself, so retries cannot resolve it and the document is dropped after paying three times.
why.B: A single corrected number hides genuine vendor errors that the business needs to see.
why.D: Computing downstream loses the document's stated total, so a vendor's arithmetic mistake becomes invisible and a missed line item looks like a valid invoice.

stem: Developers dismiss about 45% of review findings. Your bot records which findings were dismissed, but the finding text is free-form prose, so grouping 4,000 dismissals into patterns is a manual reading exercise nobody has time for. What change makes the analysis systematic?

options.text: Add a detected_pattern field naming the code construct that triggered each finding, so dismissals group by it.
Ask developers to choose a dismissal reason from a dropdown when they resolve a review comment.
Have the model attach a confidence score to each finding, then study how dismissal rates vary by band.
Have a second Claude instance read each month's dismissed findings and summarise the recurring themes.

explanation: detected_pattern records the trigger at the moment the finding is produced, so dismissal data groups by construct with no interpretation step and points straight at the prompt criteria that need work.

why.B: Puts the work on developers, who dismiss comments precisely because they do not want to spend time on them.
why.C: Confidence bands say how sure the model was, not which code construct produced the noise.
why.D: The monthly read-through is the same interpretation step performed by a model, and it still works from prose that never recorded the trigger.

stem: Your retry step resends the document, the failed extraction and the exact validation error. Which two failures is that retry likely to resolve? (Select 2)

options.text: invoice_total came back as the string "1.234,56" where the schema requires a number.
The vendor's address was placed in customer_address and the customer's in vendor_address.
due_date is null because the invoice states only "payable per the terms of our framework agreement", which is not attached.
The line items do not sum to the total printed on the invoice, because the vendor's own arithmetic is wrong.

explanation: A format mismatch and a swapped field placement are both errors the model can correct once it is told exactly what failed, because the correct facts are already in the document it has.

why.C: The value is not in the input at all, so no retry can produce it honestly.
why.D: The inconsistency is in the source document, so any extraction that satisfied the check would have to misrepresent it.

stem: Your validation-retry loop resends the document, the failed extraction and the exact validation error, and it has no cap: it retries until validation passes. Metrics show attempt 1 clears 91% of failures, attempt 2 clears a further 6%, attempt 3 clears 0.4%, and a residual 2.6% of documents have now been retried more than forty times each and dominate the pipeline's cost. What is the appropriate design?

options.text: Discard documents that fail twice, since the volume is small enough not to move aggregate accuracy.
Cap retries at two attempts, then route the documents that still fail to human review.
Relax the constraints that are failing so the residual documents validate on the first attempt.
Keep retrying but add exponential backoff so the repeated attempts cost less per hour.

explanation: The yield curve shows retries stop converting after the second attempt. Capping there bounds the cost and routes the hard documents to the only process that can resolve them.

why.A: Silently dropping documents loses data the business needs and hides a systematic failure class.
why.C: Loosening validation lets bad extractions through rather than fixing them.
why.D: Backoff changes when the money is spent, not the fact that these attempts never converge.

stem: Contracts arrive continuously through the day and your service level agreement promises extracted data within 30 hours of arrival. You want the Message Batches API for the 50% saving and you must plan against the documented worst case of up to 24 hours per batch. Which submission schedule keeps the commitment with margin for retrieval and downstream loading?

options.text: Submit a batch every 6 hours, which exactly meets the 30-hour commitment with no time left over.
Submit one batch a day at midnight, since batches in practice complete far faster than the 24-hour ceiling.
Submit a batch every 4 hours: at most 4 hours waiting plus 24 processing, leaves 2 hours of margin.
Submit a batch every 12 hours, which keeps the number of batches and polling calls manageable.

explanation: Worst case is queueing time plus processing time. A 4-hour window gives 4 + 24 = 28 hours, leaving 2 hours to retrieve results, validate them and load them downstream.

why.A: 6 + 24 = 30 hours consumes the entire commitment and leaves nothing for retrieval, validation or loading.
why.B: Worst case is 24 hours of queueing plus 24 hours of processing, which is 48 hours and misses the commitment badly.
why.D: 12 + 24 = 36 hours, over the commitment before any downstream work.

stem: A compliance audit of the week's merged pull requests must be published by Monday 09:00. The commit data is complete at Friday 18:00. You plan to run the analysis on the Message Batches API and to allow one resubmission round, also through the batch API, for requests that fail. Planning against the documented worst case of 24 hours per batch, which plan is guaranteed to meet the deadline?

options.text: Submit the first batch at Saturday 20:00 so the data is more recent, and resubmit when results return.
Submit the first batch at Friday 18:00 and budget three resubmission rounds to maximise how many requests eventually succeed.
Submit the first batch at Sunday 08:00 and handle any failures synchronously if the results arrive late.
Submit the first batch at Friday 18:00 and the resubmission as soon as results return.

explanation: Two sequential batch rounds take up to 48 hours. Starting at Friday 18:00 puts the worst case at Sunday 18:00, which is 15 hours inside the Monday 09:00 deadline.

why.A: Worst case is Saturday 20:00 plus 48 hours, which is Monday 20:00, eleven hours after publication.
why.B: Four sequential rounds is up to 96 hours, a worst case of Tuesday 18:00.
why.C: Sunday 08:00 plus 24 hours reaches Monday 08:00 with one hour left and no room for the resubmission, and the synchronous fallback abandons the saving under time pressure.

stem: You submitted 100 contracts as a single batch. 93 returned valid extractions and 7 failed because the document exceeded the model's context window. What is the correct recovery?

options.text: Reprocess the 7 through the synchronous API, since the batch run has shown it cannot handle them.
Match the 7 failures to their documents by custom_id, chunk those documents, and resubmit only them.
Match the failures by their position in the results array and resubmit them unchanged with a larger max_tokens.
Resubmit the whole batch of 100 with chunking applied to every document so the run stays uniform.

explanation: custom_id is what correlates each response with the request that produced it, so you can resubmit exactly the failures with the one modification they need.

why.A: The synchronous API has the same context limit, so those 7 fail again, and the retry gives up the 50% saving for nothing.
why.C: Positional matching is not how batch results are correlated, and max_tokens governs output length, not the input size that overflowed.
why.D: Pays for 93 successful extractions a second time and chunks documents that never needed it.

stem: Your overnight literature sweep asks the model to read a topic brief, call search_papers for whichever sub-questions it judges relevant, then write findings from what comes back. You want to move the sweep to the Message Batches API for the 50% saving. What is the blocker and the right way around it?

options.text: Poll the batch for tool_use blocks, run the searches, and submit the tool results back into the same in-flight batch request.
There is no blocker: include the search_papers tool definition in each batch request and the batch runner will execute those calls for you.
The blocker is latency variance, so keep the sweep on the synchronous API and accept the higher cost.
A batch request cannot run a tool mid-request, so stage it into two passes with the search executed in between.

explanation: The Message Batches API does not support multi-turn tool calling within a request. Staging the work into two batch passes with the tool execution in between keeps the saving on both model calls.

why.A: There is no mechanism for injecting tool results into a batch request that is already in flight.
why.B: Including a tool definition does not give the batch a way to run the tool and continue the turn.
why.C: This is an overnight sweep, so latency is not the blocker, and abandoning batch gives up the saving for no reason.

stem: You are moving a nightly documentation-coverage analysis over 5,000 source files to the Message Batches API. Which two practices are sound? (Select 2)

options.text: Have each request call the repository search tool part-way through so the model can pull in the files a module imports.
Refine the prompt against a sample of about 50 files until the output passes validation, then submit the full run.
Give every request a custom_id keyed to its file path so failures can be identified and resubmitted selectively.
Move the blocking pre-merge lint review onto the same batch, since batches usually return within the hour.

explanation: Refining on a sample raises the first-pass success rate before you pay for 5,000 requests, and custom_id is what makes selective resubmission of the failures possible.

why.A: The batch API does not support executing a tool and returning its result within a request.
why.D: Typical completion time is not a latency guarantee, and a blocking pre-merge check cannot depend on one.

stem: Your pipeline runs claude -p to implement a ticket, then continues in the same session with "now review the code you just wrote for bugs". Over six weeks that self-review has raised 41 findings, all naming, docstring and formatting issues, while QA has found four logic bugs it passed over, including an inverted permission check in code the session itself wrote. What is the most effective change?

options.text: Strengthen the self-review instruction to "assume the code you have just written contains at least one logic bug and go find it".
Run the review in a separate Claude Code instance, given only the diff and the review criteria.
Enable extended thinking on the review turn so the model reasons more deeply about its own code.
Run /compact before the review turn so the generation reasoning is condensed and the model sees the code afresh.

explanation: A session that just produced the code carries the reasoning that justified it and is unlikely to question its own decisions. An independent instance judges the code on its merits, which is what catches logic errors.

why.A: Still the same session with the same reasoning in context; a stronger instruction does not create independence.
why.C: More reasoning over the same premises does not remove the commitment to them.
why.D: Compaction reduces token usage, and the conclusions the session already reached survive the summary.

stem: A colleague proposes running three independent full-PR review passes and posting only findings that appear in at least two of them. You run the experiment across 40 pull requests: the union of the three passes contains 61 findings later confirmed as real bugs, the 2-of-3 intersection contains 28 of them, and false positives fall from 90 to 30. The team likes the precision number. What is the strongest objection?

options.text: Three full passes take three times as long and will slow down the pre-merge check.
Three passes over the same diff are not genuinely independent, since they share one prompt.
The rule discards 33 confirmed real bugs, since a genuine bug is often caught by only one pass.
Three passes cost three times as much per pull request, which is hard to justify here.

explanation: Consensus filtering suppresses true findings that only one pass detects, which is precisely what the experiment measured. Losing more than half the real bugs is not a trade a review system should make for precision.

why.A: The passes can run in parallel, and latency is not why the rule is wrong.
why.B: Separate instances carry no shared reasoning context, so they are independent in the sense that matters, and even fully independent passes suppress single-pass findings under a 2-of-3 rule.
why.D: Cost is a real concern but secondary to a rule that hides more than half the bugs.

stem: You want a quality check on extractions before records reach the ledger. The proposal is to append "now double-check each field against the document and correct anything wrong" to the end of the extraction prompt. A sample shows the model confirms 96% of its own field values, including 70% of the values a human labelled wrong. What architecture actually catches these?

options.text: A separate verification call given the document and the record, with no extraction reasoning in context.
Extend the extraction prompt with a longer per-field checklist of what to verify before returning.
Keep the self-check but have the model state a confidence score for each field, then auto-approve every field scoring above 0.9.
Run the extraction three times with the same prompt and accept the value that appears in at least two runs.

explanation: Verification has to be done by a call that is not defending an earlier decision. Giving a fresh instance the document and the record turns it into a comparison task and produces per-field disagreements you can route.

why.B: A longer checklist inside the same call does not remove the commitment to the values already produced.
why.C: The self-check already confirms its own errors, so a number attached to that same judgment inherits the same bias.
why.D: Identical prompts make correlated errors, so a majority vote confirms the mistake instead of exposing it.

stem: You split reviews of a 22-file pull request into 22 per-file passes plus one integration pass. The per-file passes are consistent and useful. The integration pass, which receives all 22 files in full again, produces the same shallow and uneven output the original single pass did. What should the integration pass receive instead?

options.text: The per-file findings summaries plus the cross-file surface: changed signatures, shared types and their call sites.
All 22 files again, with an instruction to consider only cross-file concerns on this pass.
All 22 files again, run on a model with a substantially larger context window to hold them all.
Nothing: drop the integration pass and rely on the existing test suite to catch cross-file breakage.

explanation: The integration pass is diluted for the same reason the original pass was: it is holding 22 full files. Narrowing its input to the interfaces between files, plus what the per-file passes already found, puts its attention on the relationships it exists to examine.

why.B: The instruction does not reduce how much the pass has to hold in attention, which is the actual cause.
why.C: A larger context window addresses capacity, not the quality of attention spread across 22 files.
why.D: Abandons the cross-file analysis instead of fixing it, and a test suite only catches breakage it already has cases for.
